articles.title: South Korea growth tops forecast as chip boom masks weak demand - The Japan Times
articles.summary: South Korea growth tops forecast as chip boom masks weak demand  The Japan Times
articles.full_text:
South Korea’s economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter as an artificial intelligence-fueled chip boom powered exports and investment, but a contraction in consumption underscored an increasingly uneven expansion that may complicate the trajectory for further interest-rate hikes.
Gross domestic product expanded 1% in the three months ended September from the previous quarter, the Bank of Korea said Tuesday, after growing 0.6% in the April-June period. That exceeded the median estimate of 0.8% in a Bloomberg survey of economists.
The economy grew 3.4% from a year earlier, compared with a forecast of 3.1%. This followed 3.7% year-on-year growth in the second quarter.

articles.title: South Korea Q3 GDP beats forecasts as AI chip boom boosts exports, investments - The Standard (HK)
articles.summary: South Korea Q3 GDP beats forecasts as AI chip boom boosts exports, investments  The Standard (HK)
articles.full_text:
South Korea's economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter as a global AI chip boom boosted exports and investments, advance central bank estimates showed on Tuesday, though domestic demand remained weak.
Gross domestic product expanded 1.0 percent in the July-September quarter from the preceding three months, when it grew 0.6 percent. It was stronger than a median 0.7 percent increase tipped in a Reuters poll of economists.
It was also higher than the Bank of Korea's forecast of 0.3 percent in August, when the central bank projected this year's growth at 3.3 percent. The economy is now seen growing 3.7 percent this year, if GDP in the fourth quarter stays at the same level as the third quarter.
"It is estimated that about half of economic growth is being driven by semiconductors," Lee Dong-won, director general of the Bank of Korea's economic statistics department, told a briefing.
Exports and investments are expected to remain robust in the fourth quarter, Lee said, adding that chip production volume will expand further next year while prices will continue to grow but at a slower pace.
Private consumption, which fell for the first time in nearly four years in the third quarter, will likely recover gradually, as dividend payouts by chip firms to their shareholders in the fourth quarter and bonus payments to employees in the first quarter of 2027 boost household income, Lee said.
Amid the global boom in AI investment, South Korea's exports topped US$800 billion in January to September, higher than last year's full-year record, and are on track to exceed US$1 trillion this year, which will make South Korea the fourth country to reach the milestone, after the US, China and Germany.
The Bank of Korea kept interest rates unchanged last week, after back-to-back hikes in July and September, but maintained a hawkish stance by upgrading its economic growth forecasts and remaining upbeat about the country's export momentum.
"Exports and investments are leading growth, but the downside is that private consumption remains weak compared with the overall growth momentum," said Park Sang-hyun, an economist at iM Securities.
"There could be short-term boosts, but it is difficult to expect strong momentum given labour market conditions and restrictive interest rates," Park said.
In a separate central bank survey released on Thursday, consumer sentiment fell slightly in October, as the outlook for household income and consumer spending weakened.
In the third quarter, exports rose 2.3 percent on demand for semiconductors, machinery and electric equipment, while imports grew 2.4 percent. Facilities investment jumped 4.1 percent, led by machinery such as semiconductor manufacturing equipment.
Private consumption fell 0.2 percent as financial services declined on a stock market slump and car purchases fell due to strikes at major automakers.
On a year-on-year basis, GDP grew 3.4 percent, after rising 3.7 percent in the quarter before, also stronger than economists' expectations for a 3.0 percent increase.

articles.title: In Q3, South Korea's GDP grows 1.0% and beats forecasts on semiconductor exports - Capmad
articles.summary: In Q3, South Korea's GDP grows 1.0% and beats forecasts on semiconductor exports  Capmad
articles.full_text:
The Bank of Korea (BOK) announced on 27 October that South Korea’s real gross domestic product grew by 1.0% in the third quarter from the previous three months, beating a consensus of economists centred around 0.7% and surprising markets that had expected a sharper post-spring slowdown. According to the preliminary figures released by the central bank, annual growth came in at 3.2%, above estimates of 3.0% but down from the 3.7% recorded in the previous quarter.
The release validates the BOK’s bet on an export-led recovery at a time when the global semiconductor cycle is exceptionally supportive. A survey of economists conducted ahead of the data had forecast a pick-up in activity on the back of chip exports and AI-related investment, after a 0.6% GDP increase in the second quarter. For bond investors and banks alike, the key question now is how long export momentum can offset persistent weakness in domestic demand.
The breakdown of the figures confirms that external demand remains the main growth engine. Semiconductor exports were the principal driver of the expansion, with major chipmakers such as Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix benefiting from exceptional demand for advanced memory destined for AI infrastructure. Rising orders from data centres and compute-heavy AI workloads are reinforcing an industrial specialisation that positions Seoul at the core of the global semiconductor value chain.
A chip cycle that masks domestic fragilities
Behind the headline surprise, the growth profile remains unbalanced. Domestic sectors, especially housing and household consumption, continue to underperform, increasing the economy’s dependence on external demand for chips. For the BOK, which raised its policy rate to 3.00% in late August to contain inflation and financial stability risks, this K-shaped pattern makes it harder to arbitrate between supporting activity and managing household leverage. The monetary policy board delivered a second consecutive 25 basis point hike and simultaneously revised its 2026 growth forecast up to 3.3%.
The contrast is starker given how sharply the quarterly trajectory has already turned this year. Between January and March, GDP jumped by 1.7% quarter-on-quarter, the fastest pace since 2020, before slowing to 0.6% in the second quarter, a performance that already exceeded expectations thanks to strong exports of AI-related components. The third quarter thus confirms a high but more normalised pace of expansion, running ahead of the cautious scenarios many institutions had sketched out at the start of the year.
A stronger foothold in global semiconductor trade
The current sequence is consolidating Seoul’s role as a key hub for global semiconductor flows. Recent data from investment agency Invest KOREA show that in 2024 South Korea’s semiconductor exports reached USD 141.9 billion, accounting for 20.8% of the country’s total exports and standing clearly as its largest export item. In a context of surging demand from hyperscalers and major tech groups for AI training capacity, these volumes mechanically translate into a larger contribution to GDP.
More recent customs statistics confirm that this trend has accelerated in 2026. In August, total exports surpassed USD 98.25 billion for the third month in a row, led by semiconductors whose shipments surged 209% year-on-year to a monthly record of USD 46.65 billion. The combination of higher volumes and rising contract prices helps explain why the chip industry alone could deliver the upside surprise on growth.
What the GDP beat changes for the Bank of Korea
For the BOK, stronger-than-expected GDP growth temporarily strengthens the case for the gradual tightening path it has outlined in recent months. Local analysis suggests that achieving the roughly 3.3% growth rate targeted for 2026 remains compatible with quarterly GDP increases in the 0.4–0.6% range in the second half of the year; with Q3 now exceeding that band, the door is open to at least one further rate hike if inflation fails to ease.
In the coming days, the sectoral breakdown of GDP and the BOK governor’s remarks at the October post-decision press conference will be key to gauging whether the central bank frames this upside surprise as a one-off driven by the chip cycle or as the start of a more durable expansion underpinned by stronger domestic engines.

articles.title: South Korea's Q3 GDP tops forecasts as AI chip upswing powers exports and capex - Briefs Finance
articles.summary: South Korea's Q3 GDP tops forecasts as AI chip upswing powers exports and capex  Briefs Finance
articles.full_text:
What happened
South Korea's preliminary GDP print showed a 1% increase in the quarter through September, beating expectations and building on a 0.6% rise in the spring. On a year-over-year basis, the economy expanded 3.4%, topping projections of 3.1% and coming after 3.7% in Q2.
Policymakers said this year's and next year's growth should come in well above earlier projections and will provide updated estimates on Nov. 26. The central bank noted the figures are subject to revision.
Chips are doing the heavy lifting
An AI-driven semiconductor surge is lifting exports and investment even as external risks, including the war in the Middle East, linger. The BOK said shipments and capital spending should keep posting solid advances as the chip cycle turns up, while rising incomes should slowly widen the consumption rebound.
Governor Shin Hyun Song added that the export boom is steering the country toward the 1 trillion dollar tally for exports this year for the first time. The Trade Ministry said hitting that threshold would make Korea the fourth country to do so, joining the US, China, and Germany.

Under the hood
Facility investment jumped 4.1% after a 0.2% increase in Q2, and construction investment edged up 0.7%. Before the release, Bloomberg Economics anticipated more robust outlays on leading edge chip capacity to propel the expansion.
Private consumption slipped 0.2% after a 0.4% rise in the prior quarter, while government spending climbed 1.9% following a 0.1% increase. The chip boom is feeding the public purse too: officials project national tax revenue to reach 478.6 trillion won this year - the highest on record - an outcome driven by booming chip earnings, one off dividend distributions, and brisk stock trading, and representing an increase of 28% from 2025. Seoul's plan for the coming year calls for a 12.8% increase in public spending, directing substantial resources to AI and chip infrastructure.
Prices, policy, and your portfolio
Inflation is still above target. In September, headline inflation increased 2.9% compared with a year ago; core inflation, excluding food and energy, was 2.8%. The BOK held rates at 3% last week after quarter-point moves in July and August, and Governor Shin says policy stays restrictive until inflation is clearly converging to 2%. Before the GDP print, Citigroup and Nomura penciled in 25 basis point hikes in November and February, which would bring the benchmark to 3.5%.
Why does that matter? If chip-led strength spills into wages and household spending, the case for more tightening strengthens. If it stays concentrated in tech profits, the growth impulse could be narrower. Either path will shape rate expectations, fiscal support for AI and semis, and how Korea's equity and currency markets trade from here.

articles.title: South Korea's KOSPI Breaches 6,000 Intraday as SK Hynix's $74.8 Billion Shareholder Return Plan Fuels Semiconductor Rally - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: South Korea's KOSPI Breaches 6,000 Intraday as SK Hynix's $74.8 Billion Shareholder Return Plan Fuels Semiconductor Rally  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
South Korea's KOSPI climbed back above the 6,000 mark intraday for the first time in 10 trading days, driven by a flood of buying into large-cap semiconductor stocks after SK Hynix unveiled record quarterly results and a 100 trillion won (approximately $74.8 billion) shareholder return plan. The index surged as much as 6% before giving back some of its gains in late morning trading and slipping back into the 5,900s.
According to the Korea Exchange on Oct. 28, the KOSPI hit 6,003.22 at around 10:57 a.m., up 6.47% from the previous session, breaching the 6,000 level. The index opened at 5,763.85, up 2.23% from the prior day, and quickly extended its advance. As of 11:04 a.m., it stood at 5,993.49, up 355.15 points, or 6.3%. The move followed a 3.09% gain the previous day, marking a second consecutive session of sharp gains.
As the rally accelerated, a buy-side circuit breaker was triggered on the main KOSPI market for a second straight day. At 9:54:24 a.m., when the KOSPI 200 futures index rose 5.17% to 928.02 from the previous close, program trading buy orders were suspended for five minutes. It was the first back-to-back buy-side circuit breaker since July 21-22, roughly three months ago.
SK Hynix was at the center of the day's rally. The company disclosed before the market opened that its third-quarter consolidated revenue came in at 104.6155 trillion won (approximately $78.3 billion) and operating profit at 83.3334 trillion won (approximately $62.3 billion), both all-time highs. Its operating margin reached 79.7%. The company also announced a large-scale shareholder return program that includes more than 60 trillion won (approximately $44.9 billion) in share buybacks and cancellations and more than 30 trillion won (approximately $22.4 billion) in cash dividends. The plan calls for returning most of the gains from its Kioxia investment this year to shareholders; combined with the 40 trillion won (approximately $29.9 billion) approved in August, total shareholder returns for the year will reach 100 trillion won.
Buying intensified during an earnings briefing held mid-session, where the company confirmed that demand for DRAM and high-bandwidth memory (HBM) remains solid. SK Hynix traded up 9.1% at around 1.45 million won (approximately $1,100) intraday, while SK Square also showed strength, gaining about 9%.
Samsung Electronics also jumped about 8%, reclaiming the 240,000 won (approximately $180) level. The gain was seen as front-running expectations for the company's finalized third-quarter results and shareholder return announcement scheduled for Oct. 29. Samsung Electronics preferred shares and Samsung Electronics both rose around 9%, while Samsung C&T gained 8.97% and Samsung Life Insurance climbed 9.41%. By sector, electrical and electronics led with an 8.25% gain, followed by insurance (7.0%), securities (6.02%) and distribution (5.22%). Only real estate (-0.1%) and paper and wood (-0.17%) posted slight declines.
Foreign investors and institutions drove the buying. On the main KOSPI market, foreigners net bought 639.8 billion won (approximately $478.7 million) and institutions net bought 596.4 billion won (approximately $446.2 million), while retail investors net sold 1.2346 trillion won (approximately $923.7 million), taking profits.
A tailwind from Wall Street overnight also lent support. Tech stocks drew buyers on news that AI company Anthropic filed for an initial public offering and on a large-scale AI equipment financing deal, pushing the Nasdaq Composite up 1.18% to close at 26,477.81 and the S&P 500 up 0.60% to 7,722.60. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index jumped more than 3%.
The KOSDAQ rose in tandem. At the same time, the KOSDAQ index stood at 769.86, up 26.03 points, or 3.5%, from the previous session. It opened up 1.76% and widened its gain to around 3%. Retail investors and institutions net bought 1.5 billion won (approximately $1.1 million) and 72.6 billion won (approximately $54.3 million), respectively, while foreigners net sold 68 billion won (approximately $50.9 million). Robot-related stocks stood out, with Rainbow Robotics surging 14.94% and Robotis jumping 9.76%, while Jusung Engineering (5.09%) and Ecopro (3.09%) also advanced.
In the Seoul foreign exchange market, the won-dollar exchange rate was trading at 1,335.8 won as of 11:30 a.m.
The surge comes as concerns over AI profitability that had been weighing on the semiconductor sector have eased. Anthropic's push toward a listing, Broadcom's large-scale chip contract and the strong reception to Meta's stock offering have successively lifted investor sentiment, with SK Hynix's earnings and return plan serving as the catalyst, analysts said.
Kim Dong-won, head of research at KB Securities, said, "At a time when semiconductor stocks are posting record earnings while trading at historically low valuations, the unprecedented expansion of shareholder returns at Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix is expected to be a decisive trigger for resolving undervalued corporate value."
Whether the rally can be sustained remains uncertain. Rate outlooks are murky ahead of the U.S. Federal Open Market Committee meeting, and it remains to be seen whether foreign net buying, now in its second day, will continue. The index's retreat from 6,000 back into the 5,900s intraday is also read as a sign of volatility stemming from short-term overheating.

articles.title: South Korea's 1.0% Growth Surge Driven by Semiconductors - 조선일보
articles.summary: South Korea's 1.0% Growth Surge Driven by Semiconductors  조선일보
articles.full_text:
South Korea’s third-quarter economic growth rate surpassed expectations for the third consecutive quarter, driven by sustained increases in semiconductor exports amid a U.S.-led AI (artificial intelligence) boom. The Bank of Korea announced on the 27th that the country’s real gross domestic product (GDP) grew by 1.0% quarter-on-quarter in the third quarter. This figure is more than three times the central bank’s August forecast of 0.3%. Year-on-year growth reached 3.4%, also exceeding the projected 2.6%. If this momentum continues until year-end, annual growth could approach 4%, far surpassing the Bank of Korea’s forecast of 3.3%. Lee Dong-won, head of the Economic Statistics Department 2 at the Bank of Korea, stated, “Even if fourth-quarter growth is 0%, the annual growth rate would reach approximately 3.6%. If quarter-on-quarter growth exceeds 1.4%, an annual growth rate of 4% is possible.”
Similar to the first and second quarters, exports grew by 2.3% quarter-on-quarter, led by semiconductors and other IT products, marking a higher increase than the second quarter’s 1.3%. Year-on-year export growth was 8.6%, slightly lower than the second quarter’s 8.9%. Equipment investment increased by 4.1% quarter-on-quarter and 9.4% year-on-year, driven by rising investments in semiconductor facilities. Lee Dong-won explained, “Approximately half of the overall growth originated from semiconductors.”
Despite high growth driven by exports, private consumption contracted by 0.2% quarter-on-quarter, the first decline since the fourth quarter of 2022 during the COVID-19 pandemic. In the second quarter, private consumption had increased by 0.4% due to a stock market rally and Samsung Electronics’ gift certificate redemption event, which boosted home appliance purchases. However, this effect dissipated in the third quarter. Lee Dong-won noted, “The decline was influenced by reduced brokerage fees due to falling stock market trading volumes and delayed deliveries of completed vehicles caused by strikes at passenger car manufacturers. We expect private consumption to rebound in the fourth quarter as dividend payments from semiconductor firms and performance bonuses in the first quarter of next year increase household income.” The Bank of Korea added, “Consumption of goods such as passenger cars and home appliances, as well as services like finance and food, all decreased.” Year-on-year private consumption growth was 1.1%. Government consumption rose by 1.9% quarter-on-quarter and 2.6% year-on-year, driven by increased spending on goods and health insurance benefits.
The third-quarter real gross domestic income (GDI), which reflects export prices, surged by 3.4% quarter-on-quarter due to skyrocketing semiconductor prices amid global AI development competition. While this marked a slight decline from the previous quarter’s 3.7%, it remained over three times higher than GDP growth. Year-on-year GDI growth reached 18.8%, the highest since the fourth quarter of 1977. Unlike GDP, which measures domestic production, GDI is calculated by applying the price of exports relative to imports. Although the Middle East war pushed up import oil prices, semiconductor export prices rose more sharply, sustaining high GDI growth. The gap between GDI and GDP growth widened by 15.4 percentage points year-on-year, setting a new record for the third consecutive quarter.
With inflation persistently exceeding the Bank of Korea’s 2% target and growth remaining strong in the third quarter, the likelihood of an additional benchmark interest rate hike within the year has increased. The central bank had frozen rates on October 22 after raising them twice in July and August. Governor Shin Hyun-song views the high growth driven by the “semiconductor effect” as a demand-side inflationary factor. Following the rate freeze, he stated at a press briefing, “Given that growth and inflation trends are stronger than August’s projections, maintaining the current tight monetary policy stance is necessary.” The next Monetary Policy Board meeting, the last of the year, is scheduled for November 26.

articles.title: Samsung-Backed Wooptix to Supply Wafer Metrology Equipment in South Korea - THE ELEC, Korea Electronics Industry Media
articles.summary: Samsung-Backed Wooptix to Supply Wafer Metrology Equipment in South Korea  THE ELEC, Korea Electronics Industry Media

source_detail.name: THE ELEC, Korea Electronics Industry Media

articles.full_text:
Spanish semiconductor metrology equipment maker Wooptix plans to supply its Phemet wafer metrology system to a South Korean semiconductor manufacturer. The company will begin evaluating the equipment’s suitability for customer processes next year, aiming to enter mass-production lines within two to three years. Samsung Ventures led an investment in the company last year.
“We will begin deploying equipment at customer sites next year to validate its suitability for their processes,” said Marco Franchi, technical marketing manager at Wooptix. “Our goal is to enter mass-production lines within two to three years.” He did not disclose the customer’s identity.
“South Korea is a major market, home to Samsung Electronics and SK hynix,” Franchi said. “We plan to secure logic semiconductor customers in Korea before expanding into memory.”
Phemet is an automated metrology system that measures the shape of 300-millimeter wafers, including bow and warpage. It captures an image of an entire wafer in less than one second and offers subnanometer height measurement resolution. The system illuminates the wafer with light-emitting diodes (LEDs) and calculates its surface profile from phase differences in reflected light. Wooptix calls the technology Wavefront Phase Imaging (WFPI), which applies adaptive optics technology used in astronomical telescopes to correct atmospheric distortion. The company unveiled Phemet in November 2025 and installed its first system at French semiconductor research institute CEA-Leti in May.
Wooptix is targeting logic semiconductor manufacturers first because of increasing process complexity. Wafer alignment and shape control have become more challenging with gate-all-around (GAA) transistors and backside power delivery network (BSPDN) processes. The company subsequently plans to expand into advanced packaging applications, including hybrid bonding, as well as memory semiconductors.
“Metrology can determine whether wafers are misaligned during bonding and whether the bonding process has been completed properly,” Franchi said. “In the longer term, we are also considering miniaturizing the equipment for die-to-wafer (D2W) and die-to-die (D2D) processes.”
Founded in 2016, Wooptix raised more than 10 million euros in a Series C funding round in February 2025, jointly led by Samsung Ventures and the Spanish Society for Technological Transformation (SETT). Existing investors, including Intel Capital and Tokyo Electron (TEL) Venture Capital, also participated.
Wooptix is headquartered in Tenerife, Spain, where it also operates manufacturing facilities, and maintains offices in Madrid and Grenoble, France. About 60% to 70% of its approximately 80 employees work in research and development. The company plans to expand its workforce to around 100 by the end of this year or early next year.

articles.full_text:
The Bank of Korea has found that implementing the 2050 carbon-neutrality target could reduce South Korea's gross domestic product (GDP) by more than 10% at most. The key takeaway is that while the timing of concentrated costs varies greatly depending on the pace of emissions reduction, the overall decline in the growth rate is similar.
In its "BOK Issue Note: Economic Impact of Carbon Neutrality Implementation Paths" released on the 28th, the Bank of Korea compared two implementation paths using the upper and lower bounds of the government's 2035 Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC, a 53–61% reduction from 2018 levels). The first is a linear reduction path that cuts emissions gradually to meet the 53% reduction target by 2035; the second is an early reduction path that accelerates from 2030 to achieve the 61% target by 2035. Both paths pass the 40% reduction target from 2018 levels by 2030 and reach net-zero emissions by 2050.
The GDP shock diverged by timing. Under the linear reduction path, GDP in 2050 was estimated to be 10.2% lower than the trend growth path. The early reduction path limited the decline to 8.2% in the same year. The baseline assumes average annual growth of 1% from 2025 to 2050.
| Category | 2035 | 2045 | 2050 | 2060 | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Early reduction GDP decline | 2.5% | 6.1% | 8.2% | 2.2% | 
| Linear reduction GDP decline | 2.1% | 4.7% | 10.2% | 2.5% | 
| Early reduction PPI increase | — | 3.9% | 5.1% | — | 
| Linear reduction PPI increase | — | 3.1% | 6.5% | — | 
Note: PPI figures are increases relative to the baseline trend. In 2030, both paths show a 1.3% increase.
Under the linear path, the decline more than doubles in five years, from 4.7% in 2045 to 10.2% in 2050. Under the early path, by contrast, the burden is spread relatively evenly, from 2.5% in 2035 to 8.2% in 2050. In 2030, GDP is 1.7% smaller under both paths.
Producer prices also diverge. Both paths show a 1.3% increase in 2030, but through 2045 the early reduction path has a larger increase, and by 2050 the linear path overtakes the early path at 6.5% versus 5.1%. Over the full 2025–2060 period, the average annual growth-rate drag is 0.07 percentage points under the linear path and 0.06 percentage points under the early path—not a large difference. The Producer Price Index rises by an average of 0.04 percentage points annually under both paths.
The variables driving the gap are the carbon price and the timing of low-carbon technology deployment. The carbon price, currently around $7 per ton (about 9,400 won), converges to $169 (about 230,000 won) in 2030 under both paths. After that, the early reduction path rises rapidly to $408 (about 550,000 won) in 2035 and $543 (about 730,000 won) in 2040. The linear path stays at $283 (about 380,000 won) and $444 (about 590,000 won) in those years, then surges after 2045 to $1,488 (about 2 million won) in 2050, overtaking the early path ($1,352, or about 1.8 million won). All figures are in 2010 constant dollars.
The faster-reduction path carries a heavier carbon price burden early on, but that pressure accelerates the adoption of low-carbon technology. The slower path has lighter regulation and a smaller burden early on, but technology development and deployment lag, and in 2045–2050 tighter regulation and delayed technology combine to produce a larger shock. Peak investment also differs: 45.7 trillion won (approximately $34.1 billion) in 2031–2035 under the early path, versus 43.4 trillion won (approximately $32.4 billion) in 2046–2050 under the linear path. Average annual investment in the energy supply sector rises to about 26 trillion won (approximately $19.4 billion) in 2030, more than double the current level.
The Bank of Korea did not declare one path superior. Kim Jae-yoon, a manager on the Bank of Korea's Climate Risk Analysis Team, said, "This study analyzes only the costs of carbon-neutrality policy and does not estimate the benefits," adding, "There is also prior research showing that without climate action, the growth rate would be 0.3 percentage points lower per year on average." He continued, "Early reduction has the advantage of reducing the amplitude of economic fluctuations, but it also entails significant uncertainty because investment in technology development and other areas must increase sharply," and explained, "Rather than saying which is better, we approached this as value-neutral as possible."
The estimates rest on the premise that low-carbon technology is developed and deployed on schedule. When the researchers separately calculated a case in which industrial-sector carbon-neutrality technology development is delayed by five years under the linear path, the 2050 GDP decline widened to 17.3%, about 7 percentage points larger than in the smooth case (10.2%). Most core technologies in the steel, petrochemical, and cement sectors are still in the development stage. The researchers recommended concentrating fiscal support, including the Climate Response Fund, on technology development in hard-to-abate sectors.
The sectoral impact is concentrated in carbon-intensive manufacturing and power generation. Kim noted that "both carbon-neutrality policy paths will shrink output and reduce value added in high-carbon manufacturing—refining, chemicals, cement, and steel—and in power generation." The Bank of Korea said that because the low-carbon transition may create a trade-off between price stability and economic stability, the financial sector needs to strengthen risk management.
The study did not incorporate the increased electricity demand expected from the government's three major mega-projects: semiconductors, physical artificial intelligence (AI), and AI data centers. The researchers expect that including them would require more investment in carbon-free power generation facilities and related infrastructure.

articles.title: China’s AI boom drives race for Korean memory chips as supply tightens - 매일경제
articles.summary: China’s AI boom drives race for Korean memory chips as supply tightens  매일경제
articles.full_text:
Chinese cloud service provider (CSP) giants are scrambling to secure long-term supply agreements (LTAs) of up to 10 years with South Korean chipmakers Samsung Electronics Co. and SK hynix Inc. to address memory chip shortages caused by surging domestic demand for artificial intelligence (AI).
According to semiconductor industry sources on Tuesday, Samsung Electronics and SK hynix still maintain an advantage in technology and mass-production reliability for high-performance DDR and LPDDR memory used in AI servers and other applications.
“Unlike DRAM used in PCs and smartphones, server DRAM, particularly memory used in AI data centers operating around the clock, requires higher reliability,” said an executive at a server manufacturer. “Actual performance evaluations show a significant gap between CXMT’s server DRAM and products from Samsung Electronics and SK hynix.”
Chinese CSPs continue to highly value memory products from Korean manufacturers for AI data centers, where operational stability is paramount, analysts said.
They noted that Chinese companies are seeking closer ties with Samsung Electronics and SK hynix even as they develop domestic memory supply chains involving companies such as CXMT in line with Beijing’s semiconductor localization policy.
Another factor driving Chinese companies toward Korean suppliers is the effective exclusion of U.S. chipmaker Micron Technology Inc. from China’s domestic market.
The Chinese government began imposing restrictions on Micron products in 2023, in response to U.S. government restrictions on exports of advanced semiconductors to China, prompting the company to announce its withdrawal from the Chinese market in 2025.
Chinese companies are seeking to secure not only server DDR memory but also LPDDR supplies.
DDR is a high-power memory standard designed for high-performance, large-capacity data processing in PCs and servers, while LPDDR is an ultra-low-power memory standard optimized to significantly reduce power consumption and heat generation in mobile and on-device applications.
LPDDR is also increasingly being used in servers, leading to competition between smartphone and PC manufacturers and server companies for the same limited supplies.
Daishin Securities Co. expects memory prices to continue rising as server manufacturers become willing to pay prices comparable to those of server-grade memory to secure LPDDR supplies.
Samsung Electronics and SK hynix also need to maintain steady supplies to Chinese CSPs to protect their market shares in China.
Alongside the United States, China is one of the world’s largest markets for AI data center construction.
According to a September report by semiconductor research firm SemiAnalysis, China has already built more than 24 gigawatts (GW) of AI data center capacity, the second-largest amount globally after the U.S., which has 56 GW.
China also has approximately 20 GW of additional data center capacity under construction or in the planning stages.
Among Chinese big tech companies, ByteDance is developing approximately 5.3 GW of AI data center capacity, followed by Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. with 3.9 GW, Tencent Holdings Ltd. with 2.4 GW, Baidu Inc. with 1.1 GW and Huawei Technologies Co. with 1 GW.
China’s three major telecommunications operators — China Mobile International Ltd., China Telecom Corp. and China United Network Communications Group Co. (China Unicom) — are also aggressively expanding their AI data center infrastructure.
As China’s AI data center market is growing rapidly, domestic semiconductor manufacturers are also moving to capitalize on the opportunity.
According to market data tracker Omdia, Yangtze Memory Technologies Co. (YMTC), China’s largest NAND flash memory manufacturer, captured a 38.5 percent share of the mainland Chinese market in the second quarter, overtaking Samsung Electronics and SK hynix to claim the top position.
It marked the first time a Chinese company had ranked first in the mainland memory semiconductor market.
As big tech companies in both the U.S. and China scramble to secure memory chip supplies, LTAs are becoming increasingly common.
The world’s three major memory chipmakers have announced during their earnings releases that they have signed LTAs with their key customers.
Supply agreements typically run for five years, although terms such as pricing and advance payments vary.
According to industry sources, Apple Inc. is reportedly the only company among the Magnificent Seven — Apple, Microsoft Corp., Alphabet Inc., Amazon.com Inc., Nvidia Corp., Meta Platforms Inc., and Tesla Inc. — that has yet to sign a long-term memory supply agreement.
Industry observers expect Apple to sign an LTA before the end of this year.
By Han Ji-yeon, Lee Deok-joo, and Yoon Yeon-hae

articles.title: South Korea's 1% Growth Masks Public Struggles - 조선일보
articles.summary: South Korea's 1% Growth Masks Public Struggles  조선일보
articles.full_text:
Driven by the U.S.-led AI, artificial intelligence investment boom, South Korea’s economy recorded a surprising 1% growth in the third quarter (July-September), surpassing expectations, as the semiconductor export boom continued. However, with growth concentrated in the semiconductor sector, worsening indicators in consumption, employment, and debt have widened the gap between the high growth rate and the economic conditions felt by the general public.
The Bank of Korea announced on the 27th that South Korea’s economy grew by 1.0% compared to the previous quarter in the ‘Third Quarter Real Gross Domestic Product (GDP)’. This is more than three times the 0.3% forecast released by the central bank in August. Following the first and second quarters, this marks the third consecutive quarter of ‘surprising growth’ that significantly exceeded expectations. The year-on-year growth rate was 3.4%, also surpassing the forecast of 2.6%. Even if the fourth-quarter growth rate is 0%, the annual growth rate is expected to be 3.6%, higher than the forecast of 3.3%, and if it is 1.4% or higher, annual growth in the 4% range is possible, the central bank projected.
Lee Dong-won, Head of the Bank of Korea’s Economic Statistics Division 2, stated, “About half of the overall growth came from semiconductors.”
However, as growth remained concentrated in semiconductors and the ‘warmth’ did not spread throughout the economy, private consumption decreased by 0.2% compared to the previous quarter. This is the first decline in private consumption in about four years since the fourth quarter of 2022 during the COVID-19 pandemic. The Bank of Korea noted, “Consumption of goods such as passenger vehicles and home appliances, as well as services like finance and food, all decreased.”
Employment indicators also deteriorated. According to the Ministry of Data and Statistics, the monthly average employment rate from the beginning of this year until last month was 62.8%, down by 0.1 percentage points compared to the same period last year. This is the first decline since 2020 when the COVID-19 pandemic began. While the cold winds in youth employment persist, the job situation for those in their early 60s, who have supported employment until now, is worsening. Moreover, even as semiconductor companies experiencing a boom increase production, they primarily expand facility investments rather than hiring, resulting in weak momentum for job creation.
The Bank of Korea is continuing its policy of raising the base interest rate to preemptively address the risk of high growth rates leading to inflation, price increases. As a result, loan interest rates have also risen, showing signs of increasing delinquency rates for loans, which have reached a record high. Particularly, with sluggish consumption, the delinquency rate for self-employed loans has risen significantly. According to the Financial Supervisory Service, as of the end of August, the delinquency rate for self-employed loans in the banking sector was 0.86%, up by 0.09 percentage points from the previous month, marking the highest level since May 2013.

articles.title: Musk warned of a chip glut from China in 2028, but experts aren’t so sure - Korea JoongAng Daily
articles.summary: Musk warned of a chip glut from China in 2028, but experts aren’t so sure  Korea JoongAng Daily
articles.full_text:
The logos of Korean chipmakers Samsung Electronics, left, and SK hynixYONHAP
[NEWS ANALYSIS]
Elon Musk and Jensen Huang are at odds over the future of the memory chip market. The Tesla CEO sees a potential supply glut looming after 2028, while the Nvidia CEO believes demand from a persistent AI boom will outpace supply for years to come.
GoogleAdmanager-KJD
The disagreement has rattled investors, reviving concerns over whether the massive sums being poured into AI infrastructure can sustain the semiconductor industry's extraordinary performance.
Some experts readily agree with the Nvidia chief and extend the timeline by two more years, saying supply will stay tight until at least 2030. Even then, they say, China's ability to flood the global market will be constrained by limited access to advanced chipmaking equipment, while demand from AI data centers continues to absorb much of the available supply.
“Hyperscalers are earning operating margins of 35 percent to 39 percent in their existing businesses,” said Roh Geun-chang, the CEO of Semicon Research Lab and a former head of the semiconductor research center at Hyundai Motor Securities. “Still, operating cash flow alone is not enough for them, so they are borrowing to build AI data centers, which is why free cash flow is negative. That’s a cash flow problem, not a profitability problem.”
Despite growing pushback against the AI infrastructure buildout, demand forecasts remain high, and continued AI advances mean more memory will be needed.
Musk recently took a heavy swipe at the pricing power of Samsung Electronics and SK hynix in a reply to a post warning that Korea's chip boom could face oversupply from 2029. The Tesla CEO predicted that Chinese chipmakers would begin producing large volumes of random access memory (RAM) in 2028, hinting at a threat to the dominance of the two Korean companies.
The remarks helped fuel a sell-off in Korean chip stocks on Oct. 15, with Samsung shares plunging 10.56 percent and SK hynix tumbling 12.76 percent.
Huang, however, has pushed back against fears of an impending glut, arguing that memory supplies are unlikely to exceed demand even by 2029. He also expects high bandwidth memory (HBM), a specialized type of memory essential to AI processors, to remain in heavy use for years.
Market sentiment has since rebounded following Anthropic's public filing, with Samsung shares gaining 4.23 percent and SK hynix rising 5.65 percent on Tuesday from the previous trading session.
The greater risks may lie with smaller, debt-funded cloud infrastructure providers such as CoreWeave, which have less financial flexibility than established technology giants. Some of these companies could struggle if financing becomes more expensive or AI demand falls short of expectations, potentially setting off a shakeout in the industry.
For now, however, demand for computing capacity remains robust. Executives at Amazon and Google have said their own data center capacity is fully booked, forcing them to turn to outside providers such as SpaceX to meet demand.
“Next-generation memory is increasingly complex and difficult to manufacture at economic yields,” said Song Zhe, a senior investment specialist for Asia ex-Japan and Emerging Market Equities & Greater China Equities at BNP Paribas Asset Management. “China is emerging as a serious supply-side competitor, but scaling production and climbing the technology curve will take time, particularly in HBM.”
Local media reported Tuesday that Chinese cloud service providers including Alibaba, Tencent and ByteDance are seeking long-term server memory supply deals with Samsung and SK hynix. Some have asked to extend the terms to 2035, well beyond the three-to-five years of typical long-term contracts. The products they want are server double data rate (DDR) and low-power DDR memory.
The biggest bottleneck in chip manufacturing is extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography equipment, which Chinese memory makers such as CXMT and YMTC are barred from obtaining under U.S. regulations. Even though ASML’s EUV production capacity is expected to rise from 44 units in 2025 to more than 80 in 2027, the acquisition ban would impose a substantial barrier to significant technological competitiveness for Chinese firms, according to Roh.
“The problem with the China-led supply outlook is that significantly expanding capacity requires securing chipmaking equipment, and TSMC, Samsung, SK hynix and Micron are buying up all of it,” Roh said. “Even if Chinese companies announce expansion plans, the actual increase will inevitably be very limited.”
Because of the U.S.-led ban on ASML equipment, CXMT is focusing on technologies that work around the process requiring such tools. CEO Cao Kanyu said earlier this month that the company has developed a transistor called a vertical surround-gate, which addresses longstanding problems such as electrical leakage. He said this lays the groundwork for a “4F-squared” design, and that CXMT will launch a DDR5 server memory module using it by the end of the year.
The 4F-squared design shrinks the area of a memory cell, the smallest unit that stores data in DRAM. It cuts cell area by about 33 percent from the current mainstream 6F-squared design, allowing more data on a chip of the same size. SK hynix unveiled a 4F-squared road map last year, and Samsung aims to apply it in mass production to DRAM below 10 nanometers by 2028.
Peter Lee, the managing director and head of Korea research at Citigroup Global Markets Korea Securities, said the technology “is not new.” Chinese companies have not been able to adopt EUV, so this is their only option, he said. Samsung and SK hynix can keep using EUV and do not need to move to 4F-squared right now.
“The problem with 4F-squared is that after one or two generations, it becomes hard to make the next transition,” Lee said. “To shrink further, you would need to use EUV again.”

articles.title: Korea's economy posts surprise 1% growth in Q3 propelled by semiconductor exports - Korea JoongAng Daily
articles.summary: Korea's economy posts surprise 1% growth in Q3 propelled by semiconductor exports  Korea JoongAng Daily
articles.full_text:
Gwanghwamun Square in central Seoul is crowded with visitors enjoying clear autumn weather on Oct. 25.NEWS1
Korea's economy grew a stronger-than-expected 1 percent in the third quarter, fueled by robust semiconductor exports and investment. This has put the nation’s annual growth on track to exceed the Bank of Korea's (BOK) forecast of 3.3 percent despite sluggish private consumption.
The figures were released Tuesday in the BOK's advance estimate of real GDP for the July-to-September period.
The result marked a surprise expansion of more than triple the central bank's August forecast of 0.3 percent.
Exports rose 2.3 percent from the previous quarter, led by semiconductors, contributing 1.1 percentage points to overall GDP growth. The BOK estimated that semiconductors accounted for roughly half the economy's growth in the third quarter.
Domestic demand also contributed 0.9 percentage points to growth. Facilities investment, such as spending on equipment like semiconductor manufacturing machinery, increased 4.1 percent from the previous quarter, while investment in intellectual property products rose 2.3 percent.
GoogleAdmanager-KJD
Private consumption, however, fell 0.2 percent as spending on both goods and services declined.
Strikes in the automobile industry delayed deliveries of finished vehicles, while a decline in stock trading volume from the previous quarter also weighed on consumption of financial services.
The BOK estimated that private consumption would have increased 0.4 percent without these factors.
Cumulative economic growth through the third quarter reached 3.6 percent from the same period last year, which surpasses the BOK's full-year growth forecast of 3.3 percent issued in August.
Even if the economy records zero growth in the fourth quarter from the previous quarter, annual GDP growth would still reach 3.6 percent. If fourth quarter growth reaches 1.4 percent or more, full-year growth could hit 4 percent.
The key factors for the final quarter will be whether semiconductor exports maintain their momentum and how strongly private consumption rebounds.
“Starting in the fourth quarter, semiconductor companies will begin paying cash dividends, while the recent decline in the dollar-won exchange rate, which reflects a stronger won, could significantly lower import prices and help boost consumers' purchasing power,” said Lee Dong-won, director-general of the BOK's economic statistics department.
“Performance bonuses from semiconductor companies are also due to be paid in the first quarter of next year, which should provide another boost to private consumption.”
Real gross domestic income (GDI), which measures the purchasing power of income generated through domestic production, rose 3.4 percent, far outpacing real GDP growth.
Real GDI growth tends to accelerate when raw material prices fall or export prices rise.
With semiconductor prices continuing to climb and import prices, including those of crude oil, declining, Korea's terms of trade improved further.
Real GDI surged 18.8 percent from a year earlier, the strongest increase in 48 years and nine months since the fourth quarter of 1977, when it rose 19 percent during Korea's period of rapid economic growth. Korea is also on the verge of reaching $40,000 in per capita gross national income (GNI).
“Korea's per capita GNI is virtually certain to reach the $40,000 range this year,” the Ministry of Finance and Economy said Tuesday.
It has taken Korea 12 years to reach this milestone since its per capita GNI entered the $30,000 range in 2014.
By comparison, Group of 7 countries took an average of 3.9 years to move from the $30,000 range to the $40,000 range, based on World Bank data. The transition took seven years in the United States, four years each in Japan, Italy and Germany, three years each in France and Canada and two years in Britain.
With export-led growth remaining strong and incomes also improving, the likelihood of another benchmark interest rate hike by the BOK before the end of the year has increased.
The central bank believes robust economic growth could intensify demand-side inflationary pressures.
“Core inflation next year will also likely exceed our August forecast of 2.5 percent,” BOK Gov. Shin Hyun-song said on Thursday. Core inflation excludes volatile energy and food prices.
“I believe we need to maintain our current restrictive monetary policy stance and continue responding until we are confident that inflation is steadily converging toward our 2 percent target.”

Because of the U.S. government’s export controls on advanced semiconductors to China, Samsung Electronics and SK hynix cannot export high-bandwidth memory (HBM), a key component in AI accelerators, to China. However, operating large-scale AI data centers also requires a reliable supply of general-purpose DRAM, which serves as main memory, in addition to HBM.
According to semiconductor industry sources on the 27th, as Chinese memory maker ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) rapidly ramps up DRAM production, Samsung Electronics and SK hynix still have an edge in the technology and mass-production stability of high-performance DDR and LPDDR needed for AI servers and other applications. “Unlike DRAM for PCs or smartphones, server DRAM—which operates 24 hours a day, especially DRAM for AI data centers—requires greater reliability,” an executive at a server company said. “When you assess actual performance, there is a wide gap between CXMT’s server DRAM and DRAM from Samsung and SK hynix.”
Analysts say Chinese CSPs still rate South Korean companies’ products highly for AI data centers, where stable operation is paramount. That is why they are also courting Samsung Electronics and SK hynix even as they build up a domestic memory supply chain, including CXMT, in line with the Chinese government’s policy of localizing memory semiconductors. The fact that Micron, a U.S. company, has effectively been pushed out of China’s domestic market is another reason Chinese firms are inevitably courting South Korean companies. After the Chinese government began imposing restrictions on Micron products in 2023, Micron announced in 2025 that it would withdraw from the Chinese market.
According to a September report by semiconductor industry research firm SemiAnalysis, China has already built at least 24 gigawatts (GW) of AI data center capacity. That makes it the world’s second-largest in terms of AI data center capacity, behind the United States at 56 GW. An additional approximately 20 GW of data center capacity is under construction or in the planning stages.
Among China’s Big Tech companies, ByteDance is building out about 5.3 GW of capacity, while Alibaba is pursuing 3.9 GW, Tencent 2.4 GW, Baidu 1.1 GW and Huawei 1 GW. The country’s three telecom carriers—China Mobile, China Telecom and China Unicom—are also actively building AI data centers.
This reflects the rapid growth of China’s AI data center market. Chinese semiconductor companies are sure not to miss this opportunity. According to Omdia, Yangtze Memory Technologies (YMTC), China’s leading NAND flash maker, captured 38.5% of the mainland Chinese market in the second quarter, overtaking Samsung Electronics and SK hynix to take first place. It was the first time a Chinese company had topped the mainland’s memory semiconductor market.
As not only U.S. companies but also Chinese Big Tech firms seek to secure memory semiconductors, LTAs are becoming commonplace. The three memory makers announced in their earnings reports that they had signed LTAs with all their key customers. Supply contracts typically run for five years, with terms such as supply prices and advance payments varying from deal to deal. Industry sources say Apple is the only one among the Magnificent Seven—Apple, Microsoft (MS), Alphabet, Amazon, NVIDIA, Meta and Tesla—not to have signed a long-term contract. Industry observers expect Apple to sign an LTA within the year as well.
[Reporter Han Ji-yeon / Reporter Lee Deok-ju]

[Sports Chosun Park Sang-kyung, reporter] The U.S.-Iran war, which had entered a lull, is showing signs of reigniting. The Moreno squad, preparing for two away matches in Qatar in November, is also expected to be put on high alert.
U.S. President Donald Trump stated during a campaign rally supporting Republican midterm elections in Mississippi on the 27th (Korean time), regarding the war with Iran, "It will end soon. We had a temporary ceasefire, but I didn’t like it much. I considered it a kind of waste of time."
The U.S. is showing signs of resuming attacks on Iran. The Hill, a U.S. political media outlet, cited sources to report, "The U.S. Central Command has prepared plans to conduct additional airstrikes on Iran once approved by the White House." The targets are expected to be political and military facilities in Iran’s interior.
The issue lies in Iran’s response. Since the U.S. and Israeli airstrikes began, Iran has attacked third countries hosting U.S. military bases, sparking controversy. In particular, regarding Qatar, which faces the Strait of Hormuz, Iran previously struck not only U.S. military bases but also LNG gas facilities, causing significant damage. A resumption of U.S. airstrikes could inflict further damage across the Middle East, including Qatar.
If this occurs, the South Korean national football team’s November A-match away doubleheader plans are likely to face unavoidable disruptions.
The national team, led by Robert Moreno, is scheduled to play friendly matches against Saudi Arabia and Qatar in Doha, Qatar, on November 13 and 17. Originally, the team planned to hold the doubleheader in Saudi Arabia, which will host the Asian Cup next January, but changed the venue to Doha considering the Middle East situation. Moreno, who took charge of the team under a short-term contract, is set to have his continuation until the Asian Cup decided after these two matches. However, with the Middle East situation once again shrouded in uncertainty, the possibility of the matches themselves becoming unclear cannot be ruled out.
Of course, there are alternatives. Holding the matches in a third country in Europe or Asia instead of the Middle East could be an option. However, given that the Saudi and Qatari teams are mostly composed of domestic players, the key issue is whether they can move smoothly. In particular, Saudi Arabia has recently faced significant restrictions on aircraft takeoffs and landings due to attacks by Houthi rebels on airports and oil facilities. Qatar, too, is likely to face movement issues if the U.S.-Iran war resumes, as it is difficult to escape the conflict’s influence.
At this point, changing the opponents is not easy. While it may be possible to find alternatives through various channels, whether they will serve as high-quality evaluation matches remains uncertain.
The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) announced on the 26th the confirmed venues and schedules for the Saudi Arabian Cup main round. Despite concerns from various countries, the AFC and the Asian Cup organizing committee maintain that there are no issues with holding the event as planned. Amid this, the new variable of a potential resumption of the U.S.-Iran war has emerged. In the worst-case scenario, the Moreno squad might be forced to enter the Asian Cup main round without even playing the November A-match doubleheader. This would be an awkward situation for South Korean football, which was determined to make up for its failure to qualify for the 2026 North America World Cup.
Park Sang-kyung, reporter ppark@sportschosun.com

This report is an independent strategic market study that provides a structured, commercially grounded analysis of the market for Semiconductors in South Korea. It is designed for component manufacturers, system suppliers, OEM and ODM teams, distributors, investors, and strategic entrants that need a clear view of end-use demand, design-in dynamics, manufacturing exposure, qualification burden, pricing architecture, and competitive positioning.
The analytical framework is designed to work both for a single specialized component class and for a broader electronic components category, where market structure is shaped by product architecture, performance requirements, standards compliance, design-in cycles, component dependencies, lead times, and channel control rather than by one narrow customs heading alone. It defines Semiconductors as Semiconductors are the foundational electronic components that process, store, and control electrical signals, forming the core of all modern digital and analog systems and examines the market through end-use demand, BOM and subsystem logic, fabrication and assembly stages, qualification and reliability requirements, procurement pathways, pricing layers, and country capability differences. Historical analysis typically covers 2012 to 2025, with forward-looking scenarios through 2035.
What questions this report answers
This report is designed to answer the questions that matter most to decision-makers evaluating an electronics, electrical, component, interconnect, or power-system market.
    - Market size and direction: how large the market is today, how it has developed historically, and how it is expected to evolve through the next decade.
- Scope boundaries: what exactly belongs in the market and where the boundary should be drawn relative to adjacent modules, subassemblies, systems, and finished equipment.
- Commercial segmentation: which segmentation lenses are truly decision-grade, including product type, end-use application, end-use industry, performance class, integration level, standards tier, and geography.
- Demand architecture: which OEM, industrial, telecom, mobility, energy, automation, or consumer-electronics environments create the strongest value pools, what drives adoption, and what slows redesign or qualification.
- Supply and qualification logic: how the product is sourced and manufactured, which upstream inputs and bottlenecks matter most, and how reliability, standards, and qualification shape competitive advantage.
- Pricing and economics: how prices differ across performance tiers and channels, where design-in or qualification creates stickiness, and how lead times, customization, and supply assurance affect margins.
- Competitive structure: which company archetypes matter most, how they differ in capabilities and go-to-market models, and where strategic whitespace may still exist.
- Entry and expansion priorities: where to enter first, whether to build, buy, or partner, and which countries are most suitable for manufacturing, sourcing, design-in support, or commercial expansion.
- Strategic risk: which component, standards, qualification, inventory, and demand-cycle risks must be managed to support credible entry or scaling.
What this report is about
At its core, this report explains how the market for Semiconductors actually functions. It identifies where demand originates, how supply is organized, which technological and regulatory barriers influence adoption, and how value is distributed across the value chain. Rather than describing the market only in broad terms, the study breaks it into analytically meaningful layers: product scope, segmentation, end uses, customer types, production economics, outsourcing structure, country roles, and company archetypes.
The report is particularly useful in markets where buyers are highly specialized, suppliers differ significantly in technical depth and regulatory readiness, and the commercial landscape cannot be understood only through top-line market size figures. In this context, the study is designed not only to estimate the size of the market, but to explain why the market has that size, what drives its growth, which subsegments are the most attractive, and what it takes to compete successfully within it.
Research methodology and analytical framework
The report is based on an independent analytical methodology that combines deep secondary research, structured evidence review, market reconstruction, and multi-level triangulation. The methodology is designed to support products for which there is no single clean official dataset capturing the full market in a directly usable form.
The study typically uses the following evidence hierarchy:
    - official company disclosures, manufacturing footprints, capacity announcements, and platform descriptions;
- regulatory guidance, standards, product classifications, and public framework documents;
- peer-reviewed scientific literature, technical reviews, and application-specific research publications;
- patents, conference materials, product pages, technical notes, and commercial documentation;
- public pricing references, OEM/service visibility, and channel evidence;
- official trade and statistical datasets where they are sufficiently scope-compatible;
- third-party market publications only as benchmark triangulation, not as the primary basis for the market model.
The analytical framework is built around several linked layers.
First, a scope model defines what is included in the market and what is excluded, ensuring that adjacent products, downstream finished goods, unrelated instruments, or broader chemical categories do not distort the market boundary.
Second, a demand model reconstructs the market from the perspective of consuming sectors, workflow stages, and applications. Depending on the product, this may include Central Processing Units (CPUs), Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), Memory (DRAM, NAND Flash), Power Management ICs, RF and Wireless Communication ICs, Automotive MCUs and Power Semiconductors, and Image Sensors for Cameras across Consumer Electronics, Automotive & Transportation, Industrial Automation & IoT, Telecommunications & Networking, Data Centers & Enterprise IT, Medical Devices, and Aerospace & Defense and Architecture Definition & IP Selection, IC Design & Verification, Tape-Out & Mask Making, Wafer Fabrication (Front-End), Assembly, Packaging & Test (Back-End), Quality & Reliability Qualification, and Distribution & Design-In Support. Demand is then allocated across end users, development stages, and geographic markets.
Third, a supply model evaluates how the market is served. This includes Silicon Wafers (300mm, 200mm), Specialty Gases and Chemicals, Photomasks, EDA Software & Design IP, High-Purity Target Materials, and Advanced Substrates (SOI, etc.), manufacturing technologies such as FinFET and GAA Transistor Architectures, Advanced Packaging (Chiplets, 2.5D/3D), Compound Semiconductors (SiC, GaN), Sub-5nm Process Nodes, In-Memory Computing, and Neuromorphic and Quantum Chips, quality control requirements, outsourcing and contract-manufacturing participation, distribution structure, and supply-chain concentration risks.
Fourth, a country capability model maps where the market is consumed, where production is materially feasible, where manufacturing capability is limited or emerging, and which countries function primarily as innovation hubs, supply nodes, demand centers, or import-reliant markets.
Fifth, a pricing and economics layer evaluates price corridors, cost drivers, complexity premiums, outsourcing logic, margin structure, and switching barriers. This is especially relevant in markets where product grade, purity, customization, regulatory burden, or service model materially influence economics.
Finally, a competitive intelligence layer profiles the leading company types active in the market and explains how strategic roles differ across upstream material and component suppliers, OEM and ODM partners, contract manufacturers, integrated platform players, distributors, and engineering-support providers.
Product-Specific Analytical Focus

- Key buyer types: OEM/ODM Engineering & Procurement Teams, Contract Manufacturers (EMS), Distributors & Franchised Partners, System Integrators, and Aftermarket/Spare Parts Buyers
